title: Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices, Composable: What the Evidence Says
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/29-commerce-architecture-styles/index.md, including the author's polishing of 11 November 2026) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for that the published chapter did not have: a roadmap p05, a lead sentence for the style comparison table p41, and a conclusion paragraph p65 that answers the opening; the author's two-clarification paragraph is split into p11 and p12, and p49 states the line between the vendor's inside and the merchant's own layer; see decision_log.

know: The three ideas that separate the four styles (deployment unit, data ownership, boundary enforcement) and what monolith, modular monolith, microservices and composable mean in those terms.

What the dated accounts show and do not show: Amazon (2001–2007), Zalando (2015–2025), Shopify (2019–2024), the Segment (2018) and Prime Video (2023) consolidations, and composable and MACH (2020–2026).
The costs of splitting (distribution, eventual consistency, operational complexity, and the people cost) and where each lands in Eva's order.
believe: A style is a choice about deployment units and boundaries, not about quality.
Every famous account is dated and describes a company with thousands of engineers; it gives reasons and costs, not a recipe.
For a merchant on a hosted platform the style is mostly the vendor's; what is its own is the integration layer, and its boundaries come from who owns each fact.
can_do: Answer a rebuild or 'are we behind?' question with the reference company's size, trigger and cost, and with the incidents the rebuild would have prevented.
Set the number of deployment units for their own code from the teams that must release independently, and enforce the boundaries inside one unit with a build check.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or engineering lead who has inherited a merchant's platform and is being pitched a composable or microservices rebuild (Noor Visser at Kestrel & Pine); next, the product manager or executive who must judge that pitch (Mara Lindqvist).
already_knows: Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 and January 2027 incidents in outline, the sixteen failure-pattern names and the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II to V: one owner per product attribute; prices frozen at order placement; available-to-promise; checkout creating the order once; payment stages; one order record with three status lines; invoices, payouts and the monthly match.
From Part VI: an integration style per flow with an owner, a reconciliation job, pinned API versions and sunset dates, one master per entity, one owned definition per metric; eventual consistency.
does_not_know: Architecture style, deployment unit, data ownership, boundary enforcement.
Monolith, modular monolith, microservices, composable commerce and MACH.
Packwerk, the strangler approach, Conway's observation, two-pizza teams, stream-aligned teams, serverless, hot path and verifier.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an 'are we behind?' question, the reader answers from team size, trigger and cost and sizes the merchant's own code, rather than recommending a split.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A board member forwards an article about a fashion retailer with about three thousand technology staff that left its monolith for microservices, and asks whether a brand with nine engineers on a hosted platform is behind. Using only this chapter: what is the answer, and how is it argued?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No. The retailer split because too many teams shared one codebase and blocked each other's releases (as Zalando did in 2015, when its shop teams all worked in one program; its count of more than 260 teams is from 2020; Amazon split at a traffic wall), and the splits took years and brought sprawl; an account is read for its date, the company's size, the trigger and what it paid. Nine engineers in three groups that write code and do not wait on each other need one storefront codebase and one integration service with a module per flow and a build check against new cross-module imports; a split needs a measured latency problem or teams blocking each other's releases. The brand's incidents were failures of ownership and of the joins, which a rebuild would recreate in new code.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what splitting costs in a commerce order and which boundaries exist whatever the style.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: what does splitting a commerce system into separately deployed pieces cost, where does each cost show up in an order, and which boundaries exist whatever style a merchant chooses?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Distribution (remote calls are slower and can fail), eventual consistency (the price at checkout can come from a stale copy; two channels can both sell the last unit) and operational complexity (a pipeline, monitoring and on-call per service), plus the people cost (Netflix's seven years, Uber's 2,200 services and 'networked monoliths', Segment's three engineers on 140 services). The WMS, the PSP and the carriers are other companies' systems, so the order always crosses those boundaries; the style decides how many more are added inside the merchant's own code.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what Shopify's own accounts show.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: what do Shopify's 2019–2024 accounts of its monolith show?
acceptance_criteria.expected: About a thousand developers kept one deployment unit with internal components and ownership; the boundary tool (Packwerk) found violations faster than teams could fix them, and Shopify found that its domains did not match how the code runs, though the tool stayed for holding the base layer clean; the one documented split, the Storefront Renderer, was made for a measured performance need and checked by comparing old and new responses on live traffic.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Whether to separate programs so that one team can release without waiting for another, and what each new connection costs; how to read a company's account for its date, scale, problem and limits, and what the merchant controls on a hosted platform; what an architecture style and a deployment unit are; Eva's order crossing the vendor's platform code and the merchant's integrations; the four ways a commerce system can be structured, what Amazon, Zalando and Shopify documented, and how to size modularity to the team. Evidence: dated company accounts and Kestrel & Pine's 'are we behind?' question after its rebuild proposals.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How should a commerce system be structured internally, and what do the famous examples really show?
thesis.claim: A style is a choice of deployment units, data ownership and boundary enforcement. The famous accounts show splits made when one program could not carry the traffic (Amazon, 2001) or when too many teams shared one program (Zalando, 2015), each taking years, and a thousand developers kept on one deployment unit (Shopify, 2019–2024). A merchant's own code gets one deployment unit per team that must release independently, with boundaries drawn around systems of record.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that microservices or composable commerce is the modern architecture every growing merchant should move to, as Amazon and Zalando did, so a merchant still on one platform with one codebase of its own is behind.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers a rebuild proposal by asking how many of its teams must release independently, which of its incidents the rebuild would have prevented and by when, and what the reference company's size, trigger and cost were. Kestrel & Pine's February 2027 review costed a consultancy's composable rebuild at about €3.2M over eighteen months: it would have rebuilt the platform that had held 2,300 orders in the peak hour and left the joins that failed to 'phase two'. Waypoint chose stay and surround (W4). Asked in April 2027 whether that left the company behind, Noor Visser's May 2027 memo counted nine engineers in three groups that write code, none waiting on another, and set the rule: one storefront codebase and one integration service with a module per flow (stock, orders, prices, products, returns), a build check that blocks new cross-module imports, and a measured latency problem as the only reason to split.
thesis.how_why: Each split turns a local call into a network call that can fail or arrive late, a transaction into eventual consistency and one pipeline into several to operate, and boundaries are hard to place before the domain is known. Systems copy the communication structure of the teams that build them, so a split pays when many teams block each other in one codebase, which nine engineers do not. On a hosted platform the vendor deploys the core, so the merchant's distribution cost lands in its own integration layer, and the boundaries that decide its promises (the WMS, the PSP, the carriers) exist whatever style it picks; what places them well is who owns each fact.

supporting_claims.claim: An architecture style is a choice of deployment units, data ownership and boundary enforcement, not of quality; composable is a way of buying, in which the merchant writes the joins.

The famous accounts are dated and describe large companies: Amazon split at a traffic wall (2001) and Zalando when too many teams shared one program (2015), each over years and with sprawl; Shopify kept a thousand developers on one deployment unit and learned its boundaries did not match runtime (2019–2024); the consolidations right-sized one subsystem; composable's own alliance ranks integration complexity first.

Every split costs distribution, eventual consistency, operational complexity and people; in a commerce order these land on the price, the last unit and the handoff to the warehouse, and boundaries to the WMS, PSP and carriers exist whatever the style.

A merchant's own code gets one deployment unit per team that must release independently, with boundaries drawn around systems of record, enforced cheaply inside one unit and split only on measured evidence; on a hosted platform the core and its style are the vendor's, and the merchant's distribution cost lands in its own layer.

Applied to Kestrel & Pine and to the scale stages, the rule answers 'are we behind?': one or two units through Omnichannel, one integration service for nine engineers, and a rebuild that would have prevented none of the incidents.

role.contribution: Separates the vendor's internal structure from the merchant's own code: the three ideas behind the four styles, the dated accounts read for size, trigger and cost, and the rule of one deployment unit per team that must release independently, with boundaries around systems of record.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to in-practice: the board's question, then Noor's answer

flow.rationale: The introduction runs from the hook to the two terms it needs, to Eva's order crossing the vendor's code and the merchant's integrations, to how a separation is judged and where the merchant's layer begins, and then the roadmap, so the claim about where crossings belong comes after the reader has seen a crossing. The board's question comes first in the body so every later section answers part of it. The four styles come next because the accounts are read in their terms; the dated accounts before the costs because the costs section quotes their figures and adds the people cost that Netflix, Uber and Segment recorded; the costs before the team rule because the rule sizes how many costs a team can carry; the line between the vendor's inside and the merchant's layer is drawn in Four Styles, right after composable is defined as buying, so the accounts, the costs and the rule are all read knowing whose architecture each describes; the stage table follows as its own house section because it applies the rule by size, and Noor's memo applies it to Kestrel & Pine at stage 3; the failures come after the memo, in the book's fixed order, because each is read against a style, a cost and the rule. Putting the accounts before the styles would leave 'modular monolith' and 'composable' undefined; putting the rule before the costs would give a number without its reason; putting the memo before the rule would show the answer before the reader can check it.

hook.content: A commerce team wants to release checkout changes without waiting for a catalog release. Separating the programs may help, but each new connection must carry data and handle failures, and a large company's successful redesign cannot say whether that extra work is worth it for this team.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has waited for another team's release, or read about a famous company leaving its monolith, has met the pull towards splitting a system.
bridge.to_topic: The step from that pull to the chapter's question: on a hosted platform, which separations are the vendor's and which are the merchant's, and when does a split in the merchant's own layer earn its cost?

thesis_statement.text: A style is a choice of deployment units, data ownership and boundary enforcement, not of quality. The famous accounts are dated: Amazon split when its front end could no longer scale (2001), Zalando when too many teams shared one program (2015), each over years; Shopify kept a thousand developers on one deployment unit (2019–2024). On a hosted platform the core is the vendor's, and the merchant's own code gets one deployment unit per team that must release independently, with boundaries drawn around who owns each fact.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team that wants to release checkout changes without waiting for a catalog release may gain from separate programs, but every new connection must carry data and handle failures, so whether the split is worth it depends on that team, and a large company's successful redesign cannot answer the question for it.

evidence.what: A commerce team that wants to release checkout changes without waiting for a catalog release.
evidence.shows: States the chapter's question in one ordinary case: the benefit of a split against the work each new connection adds.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An architecture style describes how a system's running programs divide work and data, and a deployment unit is a program built, tested and released as one piece; splitting one creates another program to operate and another boundary, and the work of carrying data and failures across it is the split's distribution cost.

transition_in.carries_over: Deployment units and the boundaries between them.

sections.heading: Four Styles in Plain Words
sections.controlling_idea: The four styles differ in deployment units, data ownership and boundary enforcement; a monolith is a shape, not a fault, composable describes how a merchant buys, and on a hosted platform the core is the vendor's while the merchant's own layer is the code around it.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the styles in the three terms the chapter uses and draws the line between the vendor's inside and the merchant's own layer, which the rule and the next chapter rely on.

flow.rationale: The three ideas and the table first, then the two misreadings the table invites; the composable clarification leads straight to the line between the vendor's inside and the merchant's own layer, so the accounts and costs are read knowing whose architecture each describes (the move both flow readers of round 2, and readers of round 1, asked for); the two recurring terms close the section.

transition_in.carries_over: The board's question, Kestrel & Pine's size, and the note that Noor's memo comes after the terms and evidence it uses.
transition_in.introduces: The first of those terms: the three ideas behind the four styles.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three ideas separate the styles (the deployment unit, data ownership and the boundary with its enforcement); a table compares the four styles on them with a dated example of each, and MACH, the industry label for composable, is glossed.

evidence.what: The four styles by what is deployed, who owns the data, how boundaries are enforced and a dated example.
evidence.shows: Defines each style by the three ideas before any company story.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the four styles and who owns the joins.
evidence.shows: Shows that the joins are function calls, network calls between own services, or integrations between vendors.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A monolith is not an insult: one program with one database is also the shape in which every transaction is cheapest and every fact is consistent.

transition_in.introduces: The first misreading to correct.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Composable is a different kind of thing from the other three: it describes how a merchant buys API-first products behind a storefront, so the merchant writes the joins, and the distribution costs the big companies document for microservices move to its integration layer.

transition_in.carries_over: Three styles that describe how one organization structures its own code.
transition_in.introduces: A style that describes buying.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The same split between building and buying applies to any merchant on a hosted platform: the platform's core sits outside the merchant's code, as the WMS, the PSP and the carriers do, the vendor builds and runs it and pays its distribution costs, and the merchant's costs land in the connectors, apps, themes and pipelines it builds around it.

evidence.what: Platform vendor against merchant on a hosted platform: who must be modular, the unit of change, where distribution cost lands, what microservices and composable buy.
evidence.shows: Draws the line the rule applies on.

transition_in.carries_over: Composable as buying, with the merchant writing the joins.
transition_in.introduces: The line between the vendor's inside and the merchant's own layer, set out in a table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A merchant cannot verify a vendor's internal style, so a claim such as 'built on microservices' says nothing about uptime, release cadence or the API contract, which are what to ask about.

evidence.what: Manhattan's WMS page says 'built on microservices' (November 2026).
evidence.shows: A style claim the buyer cannot use.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform's core is the vendor's.
transition_in.introduces: Why the merchant cannot check the vendor's style and what it should ask instead.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Whoever owns them, the joins between deployment units rely on two terms from earlier chapters: a system of record is the one system allowed to be right about a fact, and every style with more than one deployment unit lives with eventual consistency and needs idempotent handling.

transition_in.carries_over: The joins on both sides of the line between what the merchant owns and rents.
transition_in.introduces: The two terms every join between deployment units relies on.

sections.heading: What the Famous Examples Actually Show
sections.controlling_idea: The famous accounts, read for date, size, trigger and cost, show splits at a traffic wall or at too many teams in one program, each taking years; a refusal to split at a thousand developers; consolidations of subsystems cut too fine; and a composable style whose costs land on the merchant.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the dated evidence behind the claim that the famous accounts give reasons and costs, not a recipe.

additional_patterns.applies_to: each account: the record, then 'what this shows'

flow.rationale: The accounts run from Amazon (2001) to composable (2020–2026): Zalando's autonomy split after Amazon's traffic split, Shopify's refusal against both (its renderer before its 2024 retrospective, in date order), the consolidations as corrections of splits cut too fine, Netflix and Uber as the record of what many services cost to run, and composable last because it moves the same costs to the merchant. Each account ends with what it shows, and a one-sentence close (p35a) sets every account against a fourteen-person technology team before the costs.

transition_in.carries_over: The four styles and the terms they rest on.
transition_in.introduces: The dated accounts behind them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each famous account is dated and describes architecture that has changed since, so it is evidence that a pattern existed and worked at that date in that company, not a description of today's systems.
Amazon's front end was a two-tier monolith that could no longer scale in 2001, and it moved to a services platform of hundreds of services owned by small teams that ran what they built.

evidence.what: Jim Gray's 2006 ACM Queue conversation with Werner Vogels as digested by High Scalability (2007): 'two-tier monolith', 'in 2001 it became clear that the front-end application couldn't scale anymore', 100–150 services per page; 'you build it, you run it' (AWS, 2006); two-pizza teams; Dynamo (2007): 'well over 3 million checkouts in a single day'.
evidence.shows: The trigger was traffic, and the split was organized around small teams owning services.
evidence.source: High Scalability 2007; AWS News Blog 2006; DeCandia et al. 2007

transition_in.carries_over: How to read a dated account.
transition_in.introduces: The first account, Amazon.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Amazon account shows a split forced by traffic and organized around team ownership, but not a timeline a smaller company could copy nor anything about Amazon's retail architecture today; the evidence is two decades old.

transition_in.introduces: What it shows and does not show.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Zalando moved to microservices in 2015 not because of traffic but because too many teams shared one program, 'Jimmy', and could not move quickly.

evidence.what: Henning Jacobs (2020): Magento PHP, Java rewrite in 2010, own order and payment services 2012, 'Radical Agility' and AWS in March 2015; Zalando Engineering (2015): 'all of the Shop teams shared the same code base', slow startup and complicated deployments.
evidence.shows: The trigger was too many teams in one program.

transition_in.carries_over: A split at a traffic wall.
transition_in.introduces: A split made for team autonomy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: By 2020 Zalando's autonomy had produced more than 260 teams, 1,300 developers and 4,000 applications, and its costs: similar services in six languages, monoliths from 2010 still running, functionality built twice and principles marked as no longer current.

evidence.what: More than 260 teams, 1,300 developers, 4,000 applications; 'similar CRUD REST services written in six languages'; 'still dealt with monoliths from 2010'; the deprecated principles repository.
evidence.shows: The bill for autonomy came as sprawl.

transition_in.introduces: What autonomy produced and cost by 2020.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: From 2020 to 2025 Zalando narrowed its choices step by step: a smaller technology radar, one developer portal and, in one critical path, a synchronous read API replacing an event pipeline that fell up to 30 minutes behind at peak.

evidence.what: 2020 radar dropping Clojure, Haskell and Rust; 2023 portal replacing more than 100 interfaces; 2025 price-and-stock pipeline (>90% unchanged payloads, delays up to 30 minutes, 'competing sources of truth') replaced by a read API; about 3,000 technology employees (2025 annual report).
evidence.shows: Each fix narrowed a choice.

transition_in.introduces: The discipline that followed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Zalando shows that microservices gave team autonomy at hundreds of teams and billed it as technology sprawl, tooling sprawl and a boundary that had to be redrawn, not that microservices failed: no later fix reversed the architecture.

transition_in.introduces: What it shows and does not show.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify is the counter-example: in 2019, with over a thousand developers on one Rails codebase, it rejected microservices and regrouped the code into business components with public interfaces and data ownership.

evidence.what: Shopify Engineering (2019): 'the downsides of the monolith were outweighing the benefits'; microservices rejected for per-service pipelines, network latency and coordinated deploys; 'more modularity without more deployment units'; components with 'exclusive ownership of its associated data'; Wedge; the tax-engine payoff.
evidence.shows: Modularity was sought without more deployment units.

transition_in.introduces: A company that refused to split.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: By 2020 the components existed but every one depended on more than half of the others, and Shopify built Packwerk, a static check that blocks new boundary violations while recording the existing ones.

evidence.what: Over 2.8 million lines of Ruby, 37 components, an Architecture Guild of about 400; services split 'only for good reasons'; 'every component depended on over half of all the other components'.
evidence.shows: Ownership was declared, but the code was still tightly coupled.

transition_in.introduces: The state of the components in 2020 and the tool built to enforce them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The one documented hot path Shopify carved out, the Storefront Renderer, was split for a measured latency need behind a verifier that compared old and new responses on live traffic, not for team autonomy.

evidence.what: Rewrite from 2019; storefront code 'has much stricter performance requirements'; four to six times faster responses by August 2020; a verifier on live traffic.
evidence.shows: A split justified by measurement, not by organization.

transition_in.carries_over: Boundaries inside one deployment unit and the tool built to enforce them.
transition_in.introduces: The one piece carved out of it, and why.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2024 Packwerk retrospective reports that the tool's privacy checks were removed, that common ways of loading code were invisible to it, that isolating one base package took many months, and that the tool found problems faster than teams could fix them, so Shopify discussed removing it but kept it for holding the line at the base layer.

evidence.what: 'were removed from Packwerk with the release of version 3.0'; 'untracked and invisible to the tool'; 'a package can show zero violations and still fail at runtime'; 'took many months of hard work'.
evidence.shows: The enforced boundaries did not see how the code ran.

evidence.what: 'vastly outpaced'; 'we have discussed removing Packwerk from our monolith'; 'has provided value in holding the line against new dependencies at the base layer'.
evidence.shows: One cheap gate kept its value when the wider enforcement did not.

transition_in.carries_over: Packwerk introduced in 2020 and the renderer carved out by then.
transition_in.introduces: What the 2024 retrospective found.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The retrospective's most important finding is that Shopify's domains and their boundaries did not reflect how its code actually ran, so components became organizational groupings rather than enforced units.

evidence.what: 'domains and the boundaries between them do not reflect the way Shopify's code actually functions in practice'; 'Packwerk is a sharp knife'; 'running code, more than any metric, will always be the best indicator of real progress'.
evidence.shows: Boundaries drawn on an org chart did not match runtime coupling.

transition_in.carries_over: The tool's costs and its one benefit.
transition_in.introduces: The finding that matters most.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify shows a thousand developers kept on one deployment unit who gained from ownership and one cheap gate and learned that enforced domain boundaries did not match runtime coupling, the seven years to 2024 spent learning which modularity was worth paying for; its FY2025 annual report confirms the broad shape today.

transition_in.introduces: What it shows.

evidence.what: FY2025 10-K: multi-tenant, Rails, 'single branch', about 7,600 employees.
evidence.shows: The one-unit shape still holds.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Segment in 2018 consolidated more than 140 services, which three engineers spent most of their time keeping alive, into one service, and listed the trade-offs of doing so.

evidence.what: Over 140 services each with its own queue; three full-time engineers; diverging shared-library versions; 'the solution for us was a monolith'; weaker fault isolation as the trade-off.
evidence.shows: One subsystem had been cut too fine.

sections.heading: What Each Style Costs
sections.controlling_idea: Every split costs distribution, eventual consistency, operational complexity and people; in a commerce order these land on the price, the last unit and the handoff to the warehouse, and some boundaries exist whatever the style.

advances_thesis.how: Names the costs and where they land in Eva's order.

flow.rationale: The general trade-off and Fowler's three costs first, then the costs on three promises of Eva's order, then the boundaries no style removes, then the people cost gathered from the accounts, and finally the four styles side by side, which needs every cost already named.

transition_in.carries_over: The accounts' costs: sprawl, consolidations, the composable vendor's failure rule.
transition_in.introduces: The costs of splitting stated in general and placed in an order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Splitting a system lets teams change and deploy parts independently, but it turns some local calls into network requests that can fail or arrive late and leaves the merchant to coordinate records across systems.

Fowler named the three costs of microservices (distribution, eventual consistency and operational complexity) and warned that boundaries are hard to get right at the start, so the premium is not worth paying early.

evidence.what: Fowler, 'Microservice Trade-Offs' (2015): distribution, eventual consistency, operational complexity; 'MonolithFirst' (2015): 'even experienced architects working in familiar domains have great difficulty getting boundaries right at the beginning'.
evidence.shows: The costs and the boundary warning from a widely cited source.

transition_in.carries_over: Splitting's benefit and cost in one sentence.
transition_in.introduces: The costs as Fowler named them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In commerce those costs land on specific promises: the price at checkout, the last unit and the order's handoff to the warehouse each change when the pieces sit across deployment units.

evidence.what: Three promises of Eva's order inside one deployment unit and across several, with who pays; the Price Drift and the Black Friday Oversell as examples.
evidence.shows: Each cost becomes a broken promise and a named payer.

transition_in.introduces: Where they land in three steps of Eva's order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Some boundaries exist whatever style a merchant chooses, because the WMS, the PSP and the carriers are other companies' systems, so a style decides only how many more such boundaries the merchant creates in its own code.

transition_in.introduces: The boundaries no style removes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The people cost, which rebuild proposals usually leave out, is recorded in the accounts above: Netflix's seven-year migration, Uber's 'networked monoliths' and Segment's three engineers on 140 services.

evidence.what: Back-references to the Netflix, Uber and Segment accounts.
evidence.shows: Gathers the people cost from the accounts into the cost model.

transition_in.introduces: The cost in people and time, as the accounts recorded it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Set side by side, each style serves a different number of teams, gives price, stock and order a different consistency, and fails in its own typical way.

evidence.what: The four styles by teams served, consistency, release independence, operating cost, typical failure and when each is right.
evidence.shows: Lets the reader place a proposal in one row.

transition_in.introduces: The four styles compared on all of them.

sections.heading: Modularity Sized to the Team
sections.controlling_idea: A merchant's own code gets one deployment unit per team that must release independently, kept workable by ownership first, a cheap boundary gate and splits only on measured evidence.

advances_thesis.how: States the rule for the merchant's own code.

flow.rationale: A premise is asserted (p42: a team can carry only the boundaries it can operate), Conway and Team Topologies are the evidence (p43), and the rule follows (p44); then the three disciplines that keep one unit healthy and decide when to split. The line between the vendor and the merchant now sits in Four Styles, so the rule is read already knowing it sizes the merchant's own code. Putting the rule before Conway would state a number without its reason.

transition_in.carries_over: The costs of every split, including the people cost.
transition_in.introduces: How many boundaries a merchant's own team can carry.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Given the costs, the question is how many boundaries a merchant's own team can understand and operate, since separate services still need coordination when their owners cannot change them independently.

Every account above follows Conway's observation that systems copy the communication structure of the organizations that build them, and Team Topologies adds that teams can carry only so much complexity.

evidence.what: Conway (1968): 'are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations'; Amazon's two-pizza teams, Zalando's 260 teams and 4,000 applications, Shopify's one release train; Skelton and Pais (2019): 'teams can only handle so much complexity before breaking down'.
evidence.shows: Structure follows teams.

transition_in.carries_over: The question of how many boundaries a team can carry.
transition_in.introduces: Two observations that bear on it: Conway and Team Topologies.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The rule is one deployment unit per team that must release without waiting for another team, not per domain, flow or capability, and a second unit only when two teams that share a deployable block each other's releases.

evidence.what: Figure 3: one deployable with modules for a small team.
evidence.shows: The rule in one picture.

transition_in.introduces: The rule that follows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three disciplines from the public record keep a single deployment unit healthy for years and decide when to split it.

transition_in.introduces: What keeps one unit healthy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Decide who owns each fact before splitting anything, because in commerce the boundaries that matter are the systems of record, as Kestrel & Pine's W1 to W3 decided before any custom code moved.

evidence.what: Fowler's boundary warning and Shopify's finding that domains did not match how code ran.
evidence.shows: Ownership comes before a split.

evidence.what: W1 stock ownership, W2 one order record, W3 product information.
evidence.shows: Kestrel & Pine set its boundaries by ownership first.

transition_in.introduces: The first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Enforce boundaries cheaply by blocking new violations rather than chasing zero, as Packwerk did where it earned its keep, with a dependency check in the build of the merchant's integration code.

transition_in.introduces: The second discipline.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Split a hot path only on measured evidence and behind a verifier, as Shopify did with the Storefront Renderer; without a named measurement there is no evidence for the split.

transition_in.introduces: The third discipline.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: Through the Omnichannel stage a merchant's own code needs one deployment unit, perhaps two, with boundaries around systems of record; microservices become a real question only at Group stage, and composable fits stage 3 only as one capability at a time around a kept core.

evidence.what: The four scale stages with what is typical, what becomes necessary and the warning signs of outgrowing it.
evidence.shows: Signs a merchant can check against its own code and proposals.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Splits go wrong as distributed monoliths, half-finished migrations, boundaries in the wrong place, over-decomposed integration layers and composable without a team to own the joins, each with a sign to detect and a documented recovery.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the costs of splitting as failures a merchant can detect, and the rule's remedies as recoveries.

flow.rationale: Five failures, each named and defined, then its documented case with detection and recovery; from failures inside a company's own services to the merchant's integration layer and composable, where the chapter's reader most often meets them.

transition_in.introduces: The ways the choice goes wrong and how they map to the chapter's failure patterns.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five failures show how the choice goes wrong, and several match the chapter's failure patterns: The Giant's Boots in a small team, The Spaghetti Junction, and never The Burned Bridge as a recovery.

A distributed monolith is services that must be deployed and rolled back together, as Uber's 'networked monoliths' were in 2020, detected by releases needing several teams and recovered by merging the pair or redrawing the boundary around the data that flows, as Uber's domains did.

evidence.shows: A documented case and its recovery.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The dated accounts, the costs and the team rule meet on one line. Every split the famous companies made was paid for by teams that needed to release apart, and every cost it brought lands wherever the joins are. On a hosted platform the joins inside the core are the vendor's; the joins a merchant writes (connectors, apps, pipelines) are its own, so the style question a merchant actually faces is how many deployment units its own teams need, and the boundaries come from who owns each fact.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant can answer a rebuild proposal or an 'are we behind?' question by counting its teams that must release independently, naming the incidents the rebuild would prevent, and asking the reference company's size, trigger and cost; Kestrel & Pine's answer was one integration service and no rebuild.

callback.to: The opening's checkout team that wants to release without waiting for a catalog release, and the board's 'are we behind?' question.
callback.how: p65 answers both: a split pays when a team must release apart, and nine engineers whose groups have not blocked each other are not behind.

takeaway.content: Count the teams that must release without waiting for another; give the merchant's own code that many deployment units, with a module per flow and a build check; decide who owns each fact first; split only on a named measurement; and read every famous account for size, trigger and cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The opening's checkout team and the board's question get one answer: a split pays only when teams must release apart, its costs land wherever the joins are, and on a hosted platform the joins inside the core are the vendor's while those the merchant writes are its own, so Kestrel & Pine's nine engineers needed one shared integration service with clear owners for each fact, not a rebuild.

evidence.what: The opening case and Mara's question set against the accounts, the costs and the rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: splitting costs distribution, eventual consistency and operational complexity and boundaries are hard to place early; the documented splits followed a traffic wall or too many teams and took years; structure follows teams; composable is a buying style.
